4. The trial Court did not accept the plea on the view that the plaintiffs were not workers and decreed the suits in favor of the plaintiffs. Both the decisions were upheld on appeal. Aggrieved defendant petitioner then obtained the present rules. 

 7. Mr. Islam, however, contended that the decision in Md. Shahabuddin Vs. The Janata Bank and others (supra), though given in facts similar to those of the present case merely followed the decision in the case of the Senior Manager, Dosta Textile Mills Ltd. Ranirhat, Feni and another Vs. Sudhangsu Bikash Nath, BCR 1987 (AD) 454 = 40 DLR (AD) 45 which was a Store Keeper in the Dosta Textile Mills, an industrial unit of the Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation, was dismissed from service. He then challenged his dismissal in a suit before this civil Court. The suit was contested by the defendant, Senior Manager of the Mills, by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit was not maintainable as the plaintiff was a worker and had a remedy before the Labour Court under section 25 of the Standing Orders Act. The trial Court, however, dismissed the suit on merit but on appeal the decision was reversed and the suit decreed. The appellate decree was also confirmed by the High Court Division in revision. The unsuccessful defendant took an appeal therefrom to the Appellate Division. As the plaintiff was found to be a worker and dismissed as such under the Labour Law, a question arose whether the suit was barred or not. Their Lordships of the Appellate Division on a reference to the case of Jogesh Chandra Datta Vs. Government of Bangladesh, 30 DLR 219 held that the suit was impliedly barred because of a special remedy under section 25 of the Standing Orders Act.  In the result, the rules are made absolute and the judgment and decree of the courts below are set aside and the suits are dismissed as being barred by law. Regard being had to the facts of the case I, however, make no order as to costs.
